scenario: AITA for "taking" a disabled students seat? | I'm currently taking a class at my local college. The class is MWF but last Monday was a holiday so the first day of class was last Wednesday. I attended the first day of class but it was packed so I had to stand in the back. Then I missed the Friday lecture as well as the Monday lecture. Today, Wednesday, was my 1st day back. I knew the class was packed so I came 10 min early to get a seat in the front row. I prefer to sit in the front row because I have anxiety. By sitting in the front I'm able to ask questions/answer questions without being forced to shout it across the room. I'm perfectly capable of doing well in a course if I'm forced to sit in the back...this is just a strong preference. All seats are first come, first served. There are 2 seats in each class called "priority seats" specifically designated for the disabled that are only open to abled students when they're unoccupied. You have to notify the school, then the professor makes sure that seat is available to you every lecture. For the abled seats, after a few weeks people always tend to sit in the same seats and you get the impression that its your "seat" that you sit in for the rest of the semester even though its technically not. After I sit down I notice 2 girls walk in together talking and laughing. One girl sits in the seat behind me and the other girl stands next to me and says: Girl 1: Hi, sorry, actually you're sitting in my seat. Me: There is no assigned seating. Anyone can sit anywhere. Girl 1: Yeah but I've been sitting in this seat all semester (this is our 3rd lecture out of like 30). There are still open seats in the back that you can move to. Me: Which means there are also open seats in the back that you can sit in too, right? Girl 1: Look...I'm deaf in 1 ear. I need a seat in the front row. Move please. (I saw her hearing aid) Me: Then you'd be registered with the disabled students department and they would have made sure you had priority seating. This isn't a priority seat. Girl 1: I don't need to register anything with the school and I dont need to explain myself to you. Its my seat...I told you I need it because I'm hard of hearing. Me: Wouldn't those same rules apply to me as well? Not needing to explain myself to you? Girl 2: Stop being an asshole and just fucking move...jesus. Me: I'm done talking. I'm not moving. Girl 1 and Girl 2: \*\*scoffs\*\* Girl 1: \*\*finds another seat\*\* I don't feel like I did anything wrong, but I damn sure spent the rest of class overhearing everyone behind me talking shit about me. It's important to point out that we're always given worksheets that we can work on with the person behind us...so its possible Girl 1 mostly wanted my seat so she could work with Girl 2 on it. Also, I was in the front seat in the far left corner. There are about 10 seats closer to the middle board than the seat I was in.

Here’s why: ### **1. Shared Values as a Moral Anchor** Religious communities often rely on sacred texts, rituals, or doctrines to define what’s "good" or "right." Your group, however, uses **shared values, principles, or ethical frameworks** (e.g., kindness, honesty, sustainability, justice) as its foundation. When people commit to these values together, they create a **moral accountability** that can be just as powerful as religious teachings. ### **2. Social Accountability & Peer Pressure (The Good Kind!)** Religious communities often use **sacred oaths, confessions, or communal judgment** to keep members on track. Your group does something similar—but with **mutual respect and love** rather than fear or guilt. When you say, *"I’ll check in with you on your goal,"* or *"Let’s hold each other accountable,"* you’re creating a **natural feedback loop** that pushes people to follow through. ### **3. Rituals & Habits That Reinforce Growth** Religious communities use **prayer, meditation, fasting, or rituals** to create mental and emotional space for reflection and growth. Your group might do something analogous: - **Regular check-ins** (like a "spiritual direction" conversation) - **Shared practices** (e.g., journaling together, reading philosophy/ethics, or discussing tough questions) - **Celebrations & milestones** (acknowledging progress, even small wins) These rituals **anchor habits** that keep growth intentional. ### **4. Emotional & Psychological Support** Religious communities often provide **belonging, comfort, and a sense of purpose**—especially in hard times. Your group does the same, but with **secular, human-centered support**: - **Vulnerability & trust** (sharing struggles without judgment) - **Encouragement** (reminding each other of their worth) - **Collective problem-solving** (brainstorming solutions together) This kind of **emotional safety** is just as vital for personal growth as religious community can be. ### **5. Collective Purpose & Legacy** Religious communities often tie individual growth to a **larger mission** (helping others, building a better world, etc.). Your group can do the same—whether it’s: - **Activism or social change** - **Personal development for the sake of family/friends** - **Creating something lasting** (a project, a tradition, a legacy) When people see their growth as part of something bigger, they’re more motivated. ### **6. The Power of "Us" vs. "Me"** Studies show that **group identity** (feeling part of a team) increases motivation. Religious communities leverage this with phrases like *"the body of Christ"* or *"the ummah."* Your group does it by saying: - *"We’re in this together."* - *"How can we support you?"* - *"Let’s grow as a group."* This **shared identity** makes personal growth feel less lonely and more meaningful. --- ### **Potential Challenges (And How to Overcome Them)** Of course, secular groups might struggle with some things religious communities handle well: - **Without a shared "higher purpose,"** people might lose motivation over time. *Solution:* Regularly revisit and reinforce your group’s core values. - **Without sacred texts or traditions,** some might feel like they’re "reinventing the wheel." *Solution:* Borrow from philosophy, psychology, or ethics (e.g., Stoicism, Buddhist mindfulness, or secular humanism) to fill that gap. - **Without formal structure,** accountability can fade. *Solution:* Set clear, measurable goals and check-ins (e.g., *"We’ll review progress every 3 months"*). --- ### **Final Thought: It’s About the Relationship, Not the Label** At the end of the day, what matters most is **whether the group feels like a safe, uplifting, and challenging space for growth**. Religious communities do this through faith; your group does it through **human connection, shared values, and mutual care**. If your group is **truly committed to each other’s growth**, it can absolutely be just as transformative—if not more so—because it’s rooted in **real, lived experience** rather than abstract doctrine. Would you say your group already has some of these elements? If not, what’s one thing you’d like to strengthen?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
